steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on DivLog, a log parsing framework that prompts a large language model with in-context examples to extract log templates. Explain what log parsing is, why existing unsupervised and supervised parsers are not robust, how DivLog works and what results it gets, and end with a list of contributions.

steps.text:
1. Background: software logs and log parsing
2. Limited robustness, reason 1: unsupervised parsers rely on handcrafted features
3. Reason 2: supervised parsers restricted to their training data; requirements
4. DivLog: approach and results
5. Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
1. Background: software logs and log parsing
- modern software systems (Google Search, Bing Search, Android, Windows) essential, serve millions of users
- produce logs continuously -> downstream tasks: anomaly detection, root cause analysis, program verification
- first step = log parsing: semi-structured -> structured log messages
- manual parsing impractical (huge volume)
- automatic parsers: traditional unsupervised; deep learning (DL) based supervised
- distinguish constants vs variables without logging statements (Fig. 1)
- constants = tokens written by developers in logging statements (e.g. description of an operation); variables = run-time environment (e.g. directory path)
- constants -> log template; variables -> parameters

2. Limited robustness, reason 1: unsupervised parsers rely on handcrafted features
- existing parsers: limited robustness -> unsatisfactory accuracy on diverse logs, two reasons
- unsupervised: specially designed features/heuristics from domain knowledge (n-gram, prefix tree)
- fall short when template design does not match handcrafted features
- Drain (most widely-used): assumes leading tokens are constants, same template -> same length
- counterexample: E8 event in Proxifier, "ss.bdimg.com:80 close, 89652 bytes (87.5 KB) sent, 599249 bytes (585 KB) received, lifetime 37:51": prefix is variable (URL), length flexible (optional bracket tokens absent when under 1KB)
- preprocessing needed: regex replace common variables with "<*>"
- developers design distinct regex per dataset; regex quality strongly affects performance -> limits usability

3. Reason 2: supervised parsers restricted to their training data; requirements
- supervised parsers train models to mine data characteristics in target log samples
- training restricts models to specific training data -> sub-optimal generalization, esp. with large sample diversity
- LogPPT (state of the art): extracts a few most frequent variable tokens from adaptively selected logs -> virtual labels for training
- diverse/complex datasets like Mac: no representative logs/variables
- large variance: E253 event = one token, no variable; E277 event = 78 tokens with 36 variables
- imbalanced templates: logs per template from 1 to 166; over 50% of templates have only one log
- need: (1) automated, less human effort and domain knowledge; (2) decent results on complex data, stable across datasets

4. DivLog: approach and results
- effective, training-free; no human effort in feature design or hyperparameter tuning
- uses in-context learning (ICL) of LLMs: mines common features of related log examples in the prompt
- backbone GPT-3, first LLM to learn semantics in prompt contexts
- before parsing: select fixed amount of logs maximizing diversity -> candidate set
- during parsing: retrieve top five most relative examples + labels per target log by similarity
- special prompt format to enhance ICL for log parsing; templates without model tuning
- evaluation: 16 public datasets from LogPAI
- same-source prompt examples: 98.1% Parsing Accuracy, 92.1% Precision Template Accuracy, 92.9% Recall Template Accuracy; beats best method by 6.5%, 24.7%, 18.8%
- stable: standard deviations 3.58%, 7.66%, 7.65%

5. Contributions
- DivLog: first general log parsing framework using in-context learning, mining common patterns in prompt examples
- general prompt format controlling output structure, ensuring quality of templates from LLMs; generalizable to other prompting methods
- evaluation on 16 public datasets, three metrics; SOTA, beats all existing log parsing tools

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Modern software systems have become an essential part of our lives and serve millions of users globally. These include online services like Google Search and Bing Search and system software like Android and Windows. These systems keep producing valuable software logs, which are a rich resource for maintainers to do downstream tasks such as anomaly detection, root cause analysis, and program verification. The first step of log analysis is log parsing, which means converting semi-structured log messages into structured log messages. Parsing logs manually is impractical because of the huge volume of logs that are generated. So many data-driven automatic log parsers have been proposed, including traditional unsupervised parsers and deep learning (DL) based supervised parsers. Existing log parsers mainly distinguish between constants and variables in a log message without the guide of logging statements. As shown in Fig. 1, constants are the tokens that developers wrote in the logging statements (e.g., a description of a software operation), and variables are tokens that record run-time environments (e.g., a directory path). The constants make up a log template, and the variables are treated as parameters.

However, existing log parsers still have limited robustness, which leads to unsatisfactory accuracy on diverse logs. There are two reasons for this.

First, unsupervised log parsers use specially designed features or heuristics (e.g., n-gram, prefix tree) based on domain knowledge to extract common patterns for log parsing. Because of this they often fall short on log sources where the template design does not match the handcrafted features well. For example, Drain, the most widely-used parser, assumes that the leading tokens are constants and that logs from the same template have the same length. But these assumptions do not hold for logs from the E8 event in Proxifier, e.g., "ss.bdimg.com:80 close, 89652 bytes (87.5 KB) sent, 599249 bytes (585 KB) received, lifetime 37:51". Here the prefix is a variable (i.e., URL), and the log length is flexible because of the optional tokens in brackets (i.e., there are no bracket tokens when less than 1KB is transferred). Also, unsupervised parsers usually need preprocessing, where regex replace common variable tokens with the wildcard "<*>". The quality of the regex has a significant impact on parsing performance, so developers usually put extra effort into designing different regex for different datasets with their domain knowledge, and this limits their usability even more.

3. Reason 2: supervised parsers restricted to their training data; requirements
- supervised parsers train models to mine data characteristics in target log samples
- training restricts models to specific training data -> sub-optimal generalization, esp. with large sample diversity
- LogPPT (state of the art): extracts a few most frequent variable tokens from adaptively selected logs -> virtual labels for training
- diverse/complex datasets like Mac: no representative logs/variables
- large variance: E253 event = one token, no variable; E277 event = 78 tokens with 36 variables
- imbalanced templates: logs per template from 1 to 166; over 50% of templates have only one log
- need: (1) automated, less human effort and domain knowledge; (2) decent results on complex data, stable across datasets

4. DivLog: approach and results
- effective, training-free; no human effort in feature design or hyperparameter tuning
- uses in-context learning (ICL) of LLMs: mines common features of related log examples in the prompt
- backbone GPT-3, first LLM to learn semantics in prompt contexts
- before parsing: select fixed amount of logs maximizing diversity -> candidate set
- during parsing: retrieve top five most relative examples + labels per target log by similarity
- special prompt format to enhance ICL for log parsing; templates without model tuning
- evaluation: 16 public datasets from LogPAI
- same-source prompt examples: 98.1% Parsing Accuracy, 92.1% Precision Template Accuracy, 92.9% Recall Template Accuracy; beats best method by 6.5%, 24.7%, 18.8%
- stable: standard deviations 3.58%, 7.66%, 7.65%

5. Contributions
- DivLog: first general log parsing framework using in-context learning, mining common patterns in prompt examples
- general prompt format controlling output structure, ensuring quality of templates from LLMs; generalizable to other prompting methods

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Modern software systems have become an essential part of our lives and serve millions of users globally. These include online services like Google Search and Bing Search and system software like Android and Windows. These systems keep producing valuable software logs, which are a rich resource for maintainers to do downstream tasks such as anomaly detection, root cause analysis, and program verification. The first step of log analysis is log parsing, which means converting semi-structured log messages into structured log messages. Parsing logs manually is impractical because of the huge volume of logs that are generated. So many data-driven automatic log parsers have been proposed, including traditional unsupervised parsers and deep learning (DL) based supervised parsers. Existing log parsers mainly distinguish between constants and variables in a log message without the guide of logging statements. As shown in Fig. 1, constants are the tokens that developers wrote in the logging statements (e.g., a description of a software operation), and variables are tokens that record run-time environments (e.g., a directory path). The constants make up a log template, and the variables are treated as parameters.

However, existing log parsers still have limited robustness, which leads to unsatisfactory accuracy on diverse logs. There are two reasons for this.

First, unsupervised log parsers use specially designed features or heuristics (e.g., n-gram, prefix tree) based on domain knowledge to extract common patterns for log parsing. Because of this they often fall short on log sources where the template design does not match the handcrafted features well. For example, Drain, the most widely-used parser, assumes that the leading tokens are constants and that logs from the same template have the same length. But these assumptions do not hold for logs from the E8 event in Proxifier, e.g., "ss.bdimg.com:80 close, 89652 bytes (87.5 KB) sent, 599249 bytes (585 KB) received, lifetime 37:51". Here the prefix is a variable (i.e., URL), and the log length is flexible because of the optional tokens in brackets (i.e., there are no bracket tokens when less than 1KB is transferred). Also, unsupervised parsers usually need preprocessing, where regex replace common variable tokens with the wildcard "<*>". The quality of the regex has a significant impact on parsing performance, so developers usually put extra effort into designing different regex for different datasets with their domain knowledge, and this limits their usability even more.

Second, existing supervised log parsers usually need to train models to mine the data characteristics in target log samples. This training process can restrict the models to the specific training data, and this leads to sub-optimal generalization performance across the overall dataset, especially when the dataset has a lot of sample diversity. For instance, LogPPT, the state-of-the-art parser, extracts a few of the most frequent variable tokens from adaptively selected logs and uses them to generate virtual labels for model training. But for diverse and complex datasets like Mac there might be no representative logs or variables for the overall dataset. This is because the dataset contains a large variance of logs and variables (e.g., the E253 event only contains one token without a variable, while the E277 event contains 78 tokens with 36 variables) and an imbalanced template distribution (e.g., the number of logs in each template ranges from 1 to 166, and over 50% of templates contain only one log). Overall, there is a pressing need for a more effective log parsing technique that meets these requirements: (1) It is automated enough to reduce the human effort and domain knowledge involved. (2) It shows decent results on complex data and is stable across various log datasets.

For this purpose, this paper proposes DivLog, an effective log parsing framework that is training-free and does not need human effort in feature design or hyperparameter tuning. DivLog uses the in-context learning (ICL) ability of large language models (LLMs) to generate log templates by mining the common features of related log examples in the prompt. Specifically, DivLog uses GPT-3 as the backbone, which is the first LLM that showed the ability to learn semantics in prompt contexts. Before log parsing, DivLog selects a fixed amount of logs by explicitly maximizing their diversity, and builds a candidate set from them for the prompting later. During parsing, for each target log it retrieves the top five most relative log examples and their labels from the candidate set based on their similarity. Then DivLog puts them into a special prompt format, which is designed to improve ICL performance for log parsing. Guided by the examples and their labels in the prompt, DivLog generates log templates without needing model tuning. We evaluated DivLog on 16 public datasets from LogPAI. The results show that when the prompt examples come from the same log source as the target log message, DivLog achieves (1) 98.1% Parsing Accuracy, (2) 92.1% Precision Template Accuracy, and (3) 92.9% Recall Template Accuracy, which is better than the current best method by 6.5%, 24.7%, 18.8%, respectively. DivLog also has stable parsing quality across the 16 datasets, and the standard deviations for the three accuracy metrics are only 3.58%, 7.66%, and 7.65%.

The main contributions of this paper are:

- • It proposes DivLog, which is the first general log parsing framework that uses the in-context learning ability for log parsing by mining common patterns in prompt examples.

- • It designs a general prompt format that explicitly controls the output structure and ensures the quality of the log templates generated by LLMs, and this format can be generalized to improve other prompting methods.

- • It evaluates DivLog on 16 public datasets with three different metrics. The results show that DivLog achieves SOTA performance and outperforms all existing log parsing tools.

First, unsupervised log parsers utilize specially designed features or heuristics (e.g., n-gram [13], prefix tree [12,14]) based on domain knowledge to extract common patterns for log parsing. As a result, they often fall short on log sources whose template design does not match well with the handcrafted features. For example, the most widely-used parser, Drain [14], assumes that leading tokens are constants and that logs from the same template share the same length. However, these assumptions are inadequate for logs from the E8 event in Proxifier [19], e.g., "ss.bdimg.com:80 close, 89652 bytes (87.5 KB) sent, 599249 bytes (585 KB) received, lifetime 37:51", where the prefix is a variable (i.e., URL) and the log length is flexible due to the optional tokens in brackets (i.e., no bracket tokens when the transferred bytes are less than 1KB). Moreover, unsupervised parsers usually need preprocessing [10], in which regex replace common variable tokens with the wildcard "<*>". Because regex quality has a significant impact on parsing performance [20], developers typically invest extra effort in designing distinct regex for different datasets with their domain knowledge, which further limits their usability.

Second, existing supervised log parsers typically need to train models to mine the data characteristics in target log samples [16,17]. This training process may restrict the models to the specific training data, leading to sub-optimal generalization performance across the overall dataset, especially when the dataset exhibits significant sample diversity. For instance, the state-of-the-art parser, LogPPT [17], extracts a few of the most frequent variable tokens from adaptively selected logs to generate virtual labels for model training. However, for diverse and complex datasets such as Mac [19], there might be no representative logs or variables for the overall dataset, since the dataset contains a large variance of logs and variables (e.g., the E253 event only contains one token without a variable, while the E277 event contains 78 tokens with 36 variables) and an imbalanced template distribution (e.g., the number of logs in each template ranges from 1 to 166, with over 50% of templates containing only one log). Overall, there is a pressing need for a more effective log parsing technique that meets the following requirements: (1) Sufficiently automated to reduce the human effort and domain knowledge involved. (2) Demonstrates decent results on complex data and ensures stability across various log datasets.

To this end, this paper proposes DivLog, an effective and training-free log parsing framework that requires no human effort in feature design or hyperparameter tuning. DivLog adopts the in-context learning (ICL) ability of large language models (LLMs) [21] to generate log templates by mining the common features of related log examples in the prompt. Specifically, DivLog employs GPT-3 [22] as the backbone, the first LLM that exhibits the ability to learn semantics in prompt contexts. Before log parsing, DivLog selects a fixed amount of logs by explicitly maximizing their diversity to build a candidate set for subsequent prompting. During parsing, it retrieves the top five most relative log examples and their labels from the candidate set for each target log based on their similarity. DivLog then organizes them in a special prompt format designed to enhance ICL performance for log parsing. With the guidance of the examples and their labels in the prompt, DivLog generates log templates without necessitating model tuning. DivLog has been evaluated on 16 public datasets from LogPAI [18]. The results show that, when using prompt examples from the same log source as the target log message, DivLog achieves (1) 98.1% Parsing Accuracy, (2) 92.1% Precision Template Accuracy, and (3) 92.9% Recall Template Accuracy, outperforming the current best method by 6.5%, 24.7%, 18.8%, respectively. Furthermore, DivLog exhibits stable parsing quality across the 16 different datasets, with standard deviations of only 3.58%, 7.66%, and 7.65% for the three accuracy metrics.

This paper makes the following main contributions:

- • It proposes DivLog, the first general log parsing framework that exploits in-context learning ability for log parsing by mining common patterns in prompt examples.

- • It designs a general prompt format that explicitly controls the output structure and ensures the quality of the log templates generated by LLMs, and which can be generalized to enhance other prompting methods.

- • It presents an evaluation of DivLog on 16 public datasets using three different metrics. The results show that DivLog achieves SOTA performance, outperforming all existing log parsing tools.
